summary: TANAW, developed by Project Gravensoft, is an open-source geospatial web application for exploring NASA–ISRO NISAR radar observations over CAMANAVA and the nearby Bulacan coast. It maps open water outside the usual water mask during the 2026 wet season and combines these observations with NASA GPM IMERG rainfall timing and NASA POWER rainfall history from 2000 onward. Users can compare satellite passes, search cities and barangays, inspect local observations, and export briefings and data. Seasonal outlooks and conditional rainfall scenarios provide future context. TANAW makes complex Earth-observation data more accessible to researchers and students while clearly explaining limitations: the current water layer does not reliably detect flooded streets, and ground-motion results remain unavailable.
details:
TANAW addresses the “Dancing with the SARs” challenge by making NISAR radar observations accessible through an interactive map of CAMANAVA and the nearby Bulacan coast. Users can compare observations from the 2026 wet season, inspect open water outside the usual water mask, explore radar backscatter and polarization, search cities and barangays, and export location-specific briefings and CSV data.

The system combines NISAR observations with NASA GPM IMERG rainfall timing, NASA POWER rainfall history from 2000 onward, land cover, administrative boundaries, population estimates, and building footprints. The historical timeline distinguishes dataset availability from imagery the application actually processed. Seasonal outlooks and conditional rainfall scenarios provide additional future context.

The application uses a Next.js and React frontend, Leaflet mapping, and a Python FastAPI backend. Processing scripts prepare the observations and cache results for the application. A public data package and setup instructions support running the system locally.

Our intended users are researchers and students exploring relationships between satellite observations, rainfall, and environmental conditions. TANAW’s creative approach combines comparisons, place-based explanations, bilingual briefings and an educational “How radar sees” guide with visible sources and limitations.

Scientific transparency guides the interpretation. The open-water method can miss flooded urban streets, and usable ground-motion results remain unavailable. IMERG and POWER rainfall estimates represent coarse grid cells. Population exposure is an estimate, not measured damage.
